A A About Research Grants Blog Contact Careers Home About Research Grants Blog Careers Blog Organisation Towards technical best practice for frontier AI development Our view on the emerging challenges facing frontier AI organisations, the technical practices most urgently needed to meet them, and how we will work with industry and others to develop them. — Oct 12, 2026 On 22 September, the Prime Minister set out steps the UK is taking to ensure AI delivers on its vast potential for good. These include a commitment to work towards principles and standards that ensure the most capable AI systems are developed securely and with appropriate transparency. The AI Security Institute (AISI) will play a key role in delivering that commitment, with partners across industry, governments and beyond. This work responds to continued, rapid AI capability progress in recent months. That progress promises a wide range of benefits, but it has also outpaced several practices used to manage risk and oversee frontier systems – especially with risks now emerging earlier, during AI development itself. Here we set out AISI’s view of these challenges and the new technical practices and controls most urgently needed to address them. title: Large Language Models for Machine Translation Quality Annotation: Humans and Models Are Both Challenged
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are considered to be a more efficient and cost-effective alternative to human judgment for Machine Translation (MT) evaluation. With MT evaluation spanning a large number of language pairs, domains and levels of annotation granularity, LLMs must be thoroughly evaluated across these dimensions before being reliably used as alternatives to human evaluation. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of LLMs for two prominent MT quality evaluation schemes: Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) and Error Span Annotation (ESA) by comparing their agreement with human…

title: Self-Compacting Language Model Agents
summary: Long agent traces composed of chains of thought and tool calls accumulate stale content that anchor subsequent generations, and eventually outgrow the context window. Existing scaffolds mitigate it with fixed-interval compaction triggered at a token threshold. Such triggers pay no heed to trajectory structure, risking discard of partial results mid-derivation or mid-search. We propose SELFCOMPACT, a scaffold that allows the model itself to decide when and how to compact. title: Minions: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices
summary: The increasing demand for GPU-accelerated machine learning inference has exposed limitations in centralized GPU infrastructures, including high cost, limited elasticity, and long wait times under resource constraints. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon–based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. summary: StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutoring tools before they are tested with learners. title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
summary: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators. OpenAI said that the three employees “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures,” before doubling down on X without providing further evidence . The three dispute the claim and say that “at no point do we believe we engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.” Jasmine Wang said she accidentally opened an executive email (still available to her due to an OpenAI IT error) and reported it within minutes. title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
summary: Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) generates text from coarse concepts to fine details in a handful of parallel steps, matching or beating strong diffusion language models while running 10–31× faster and training on 4–5× fewer tokens.
